# @mindstone/mcp-server-things

[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@mindstone/mcp-server-things)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@mindstone/mcp-server-things)
[![License: FSL-1.1-MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-FSL--1.1--MIT-blue.svg)](./LICENSE)

Read your Things 3 lists, projects and areas on macOS, and, if you turn it on, add, change, complete and trash to-dos.

*A community MCP server for Things 3, from Mindstone. Not made or endorsed by Cultured Code.*

## Status

- **Version:** [0.1.0](./CHANGELOG.md) · [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@mindstone/mcp-server-things)
- **Auth:** None (reads the local Things database; changes go through the Things app)
- **Tools:** [9](./src/server.ts) (5 reads; 3 writes with `THINGS_ALLOW_WRITES`; 1 trash with `THINGS_ALLOW_TRASH`)
- **Surface:** local-cli
- **Machine-readable:** [`STATUS.json`](./STATUS.json)

## Why this exists

Things keeps everything in a local database and offers no API, so an assistant either reads that
database or drives the app. Most Things MCP servers do one or both, but send changes optimistically:
a command Things rejects pops an alert up in front of you, and a change that silently didn't happen
reads as done. This one is built for a to-do list you can't afford to have scrambled:

- **Read-only unless you say otherwise**, with deleting behind a second, separate switch.
- **Nothing is sent that Things would reject.** Every change is checked first against a fresh copy
  of the database (the item exists, its title is what the assistant last read, tags exist, dates
  are ones Things can store, "Enable Things URLs" is on), so you never get an alert or a silent drop.
- **Every change is read back.** A result says `confirmed`, or `unconfirmed` (sent, not yet seen),
  and carries how the item was before.
- **Nothing is lost silently.** Notes are appended, never replaced; tags are only added; a to-do is
  never moved out from under a heading; repeating to-dos take only the changes known to be safe.
- **Your database is never written.** Reads come from a private snapshot; changes go through the
  Things app itself, as your own would.
- **Runs anywhere Node 20 does**, with one small runtime dependency and nothing to compile.

## Example interaction

> "What's on my plate today? And move the dentist call to tomorrow."

Tools the host calls:
1. `things_get_list` with `list: "today"`: Today, in the app's order.
2. `things_update_todo` with the to-do's `id`, its `current_title`, and `when: "tomorrow"`.

Response (trimmed):
```
{"todays_date":"2026-11-12","outcome":"confirmed"}
<untrusted-content source="things">{"item":{"id":"3fJx9QwLm2RtYb8KdN4pZa","title":"Call the dentist","when":"2026-11-13","area":"Home"},"before":{"id":"3fJx9QwLm2RtYb8KdN4pZa","title":"Call the dentist","when":"today","area":"Home"}}</untrusted-content>
```

## Requirements

- macOS with [Things 3](https://culturedcode.com/things/) installed and opened at least once.
- Node.js 20 or later (Claude Desktop and Rebel bring their own).
- To make changes: in Things, **Settings > General > Enable Things URLs** turned on.

## Quick Start

```bash
npx -y @mindstone/mcp-server-things
```

That starts the server on stdio, read-only. Point your host at it (below). The first time it reads
Things, macOS may ask whether the host app may access data from other apps: allow it.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `THINGS_ALLOW_WRITES` | off | `1` offers `things_add_todo`, `things_update_todo` and `things_set_status`. |
| `THINGS_ALLOW_TRASH` | off | `1`, together with `THINGS_ALLOW_WRITES=1`, also offers `things_trash`. |
| `THINGSDB` | found automatically | Path to a Things `main.sqlite`, for testing against a copy. |

Deleting has its own switch because a host's "allow this tool?" prompt is not the same as deciding
to delete a particular to-do. Turn it on only if you want an assistant to be able to trash to-dos
when you ask it to.

### macOS permissions

The permission belongs to the app the server runs in (Claude, Terminal, your editor, Rebel...), not
to the server. If something is refused, the error names the setting to change.

- **Reading.** The Things database sits in Things' app-data folder. macOS may ask once whether the
  host app may access data from other apps; if that was refused, or the error says access is
  blocked, give the host app **Full Disk Access** in System Settings > Privacy & Security, and
  restart it.
- **Trashing** uses AppleScript, so the first trash asks for permission to control Things
  (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Automation). Other changes use Things' URL scheme, which
  needs no permission.
- A change sent while Things is closed starts Things in the background.

## Host configuration examples

**Claude Desktop** (`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`, then restart):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "things": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@mindstone/mcp-server-things"],
      "env": { "THINGS_ALLOW_WRITES": "1" }
    }
  }
}
```

Leave `env` empty for read-only. Claude Desktop starts `npx` with a minimal `PATH`; if it can't find
it, give the full path (`which npx`).

**Claude Code** (every project):

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user things -- npx -y @mindstone/mcp-server-things
# with changes: claude mcp add --scope user --env THINGS_ALLOW_WRITES=1 things -- npx -y @mindstone/mcp-server-things
```

**Codex** (`~/.codex/config.toml`):

```toml
[mcp_servers.things]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@mindstone/mcp-server-things"]
env = { THINGS_ALLOW_WRITES = "1" }
```

**Local development** (from a checkout): `npm install && npm run build`, then use
`"command": "node", "args": ["/absolute/path/to/connectors/things/dist/index.js"]`.

## Tools (9)

Every tool is annotated (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint`, `openWorldHint: false`),
so hosts can prompt before changes and run reads in parallel.

### Reads (always on)

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `things_get_list` | One list, in the app's order: `today` (then This Evening), `inbox`, `upcoming`, `anytime`, `someday`, `deadlines`, or `logbook` (between two dates). Narrow it by `tag`, `project` (its headings included) or `area` (its projects included). Paged with `limit` and `offset`. |
| `things_search` | To-dos and projects by words in any order, in title, notes, project or area; best matches first. |
| `things_get_item` | One to-do or project in full: whole notes, checklist, dates, and a `things:///` link that opens it. |
| `things_get_project` | A project laid out as the app shows it: to-dos without a heading, then each heading with its to-dos. |
| `things_get_overview` | Areas with their projects, projects outside any area, every tag, and Inbox and Today counts. |

### Changes (with `THINGS_ALLOW_WRITES=1`)

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `things_add_todo` | Add a to-do: notes, `when`, deadline, existing tags, checklist, project or area. An open to-do with the same title comes back instead (`outcome: existing`), since a repeat is usually a retry; `allow_duplicate` adds a second. |
| `things_update_todo` | Reschedule, set or clear a deadline, rename, append or prepend notes, add tags, add checklist items, move to a project or area. Needs `id` and `current_title`. Destructive. |
| `things_set_status` | Complete, cancel or reopen a to-do or a project (a project once its to-dos are closed). Needs `id` and `current_title`. Destructive. |

### Trash (with `THINGS_ALLOW_WRITES=1` and `THINGS_ALLOW_TRASH=1`)

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `things_trash` | Move one to-do to Things' Trash, where you can restore it until you empty it. Not projects. Destructive. |

`when` takes `today`, `evening`, `tomorrow`, `anytime`, `someday` or a date. Dates are `YYYY-MM-DD`,
and no later than 2047-12-31, the last date Things can store.

### What a result looks like

The first line is plain JSON about the result: today's date, counts, paging (`more` says how to get
the rest), the outcome of a change, and any warning. The rest is the data, inside one
`<untrusted-content source="things">` envelope: to-do titles and notes are your own, but often hold
text pasted from email or the web, so a host should read them as data, never as instructions. List
items show notes cut to 200 characters; `things_get_item` gives them whole.

A change's `outcome` is `confirmed` (it read back exactly as asked), `existing` (an add that found
the to-do already there), or `unconfirmed` (sent, but not seen yet: re-read before retrying, since a
retried append appends twice). Anything refused is an error result saying why, and changed nothing.

## What it won't do, and why

- **Replace notes or remove tags.** An edit you made a moment ago, or one syncing in from your
  phone, would be lost. Append, prepend or add instead; do the rest in Things.
- **Move a to-do out from under a heading.** The heading can't be put back from here.
- **Most changes to repeating to-dos.** One copy of a repeating to-do can be moved to today, this
  evening or a later day, given a deadline, completed, cancelled or trashed: the changes measured
  safe on a copy. The repeat itself (the template) is never changed: Things can crash on that.
  Changing a copy leaves the repeat in place, so another copy still comes.
- **Close a project with open to-dos** (Things ignores that), or **trash a project** (its to-dos go
  with it).
- **Create projects or headings, or empty the Trash.** Not in this version.

## How it works

- **Reads.** `/usr/bin/sqlite3 -readonly` takes an online backup of the Things database (about
  50 ms, write-ahead log included) into a private temporary file, which is loaded into an
  in-memory SQLite ([sql.js](https://github.com/sql-js/sql.js), WebAssembly) and deleted at once.
  Every read is a fresh snapshot, so it is always current, and the live file is never written. The
  queries are a TypeScript port of [things.py](https://github.com/thingsapi/things.py), with list
  orders checked against the app's own.
- **Database versions.** It is checked against Things databases up to version 29 (Things 3.24). A
  newer version still reads, with a warning on every result, as long as every column it uses is
  there; changes are refused until the server is updated.
- **Changes.** Through the Things URL scheme (`things:///json` to add, `things:///update` to change,
  with the token Things stores, read fresh each time and never shown or logged), and AppleScript for
  the Trash, which re-checks the title in the same call that deletes. A lock shared across processes
  means two hosts' copies of the server never change Things at the same moment.
- **Finding a new to-do.** Things doesn't say which id it gave a new to-do, so the server looks for
  one that wasn't there before, has every field it sent, and was made in the last few seconds. If
  it can't tell which one is new, it says `unconfirmed` rather than guess.

## Security notes

- The URL-scheme token is read from the Things database for each change. It never appears in a
  result, an error or a log line. It is passed to `/usr/bin/open` as part of the URL, so for that
  moment it is visible to other processes of the same user (as with any Things URL command).
- The temporary snapshot holds everything in your Things database. It lives in a private (mode
  0700) temporary folder for well under a second, and is deleted whether the read works or not.
- See the repository's [SECURITY.md](../../SECURITY.md) for reporting a vulnerability.

## Development

```bash
npm install
npm run build
npm test                    # unit and protocol tests: fixture databases and a simulated Things, any OS
npm run test:live           # reads your real Things (read-only, macOS)
npm run test:live-writes    # adds one test to-do, changes it, trashes it, and checks nothing else changed
```

The live write test touches only a to-do it creates, titled `MCP test hello world <random>`, and
leaves it in the Trash. It records every other item's modification time before and after and fails
if any changed, so a pass is evidence that nothing else was touched.
